slides: Open by framing differential geometry of curves as geometry seen from a moving observer traveling along the curve. The chapter converts vector products, derivatives, curvature, evolutes, involutes, and helices into local measurements that can be checked point by point.

Use the route slide to establish the sequence from algebraic vector products to moving frames. Each section adds one measuring tool: projections and volumes, derivatives of vector functions, curvature and centers, involute companions, Frenet frames, and helix diagnostics.

The vector product slide grounds the chapter in algebraic measurements. Dot products give projection data, cross products and Gram determinants give the same area, and the signed triple product matches the Gram volume, so later curve formulas rest on verified vector identities.

A unit vector function can move while keeping constant length, and the derivative must be perpendicular to the position vector. The samples all have speed one and zero dot product with the derivative, while radial acceleration points inward with dot product minus one.

Curvature becomes visible when the ellipse is paired with its evolute. The sampled curvature varies from about zero point two three eight to one point six six three, and the numerical evolute agrees with the formula to roundoff, making centers of curvature concrete.

The catenary and tractrix slide should emphasize companion curves rather than isolated formulas. The tractrix sample keeps tangent length to the x-axis equal to one at every listed point, with zero maximum error, making the involute-style constraint inspectable.

The circular helix is the first full three-dimensional moving-frame laboratory. Curvature and torsion are nearly constant, the numerical means match the exact values closely, and the Frenet frame remains orthogonal to roundoff as it travels around the helix.

General helices and concho-spirals extend the helix idea by replacing one explicit curve with diagnostic ratios. The tangent angle standard deviation is essentially zero, the kappa over tau ratio is stable, and the cone ratio z over radius has roundoff-level variation.

Frame this slide as the conceptual summary of the chapter. A curve is no longer just a trace in space; it carries a tangent, normal, binormal, curvature, torsion, and associated companion curves, each of which can be tested through local vector identities.

Close by connecting the chapter to the next surface chapters. Curves teach the habit of extracting geometry from derivatives and frames; surfaces will reuse that habit with two parameters, normal curvature, principal directions, geodesics, and intrinsic curvature.
